projects.title: SEO audit and content plan for a real website
projects.summary: Audit the SEO of a small real website (a local business, an association, a friend’s shop) and write a prioritised plan: technical fixes, keywords, and three content briefs.
projects.why: SEO roles ask for proof that you can find what holds a site back and decide what to do first. A real audit with screenshots, a clear priority list and briefs a writer could use shows exactly that, and the site owner can be your reference.

data.name: Google Search Central
data.note: Google’s SEO Starter Guide: the reference for titles, content, links and what to avoid.

data.name: Search Console Help
data.note: Queries, pages and indexing reports, if the site owner gives you access.

data.name: Google Trends
data.note: Compare search interest for topics and keywords over time and by region, for free.

steps.title: Pick a site and set the goal
steps.text: Choose a small site whose owner agrees to the audit. Write down its goal (calls, bookings, sales), its audience and three competitors that rank above it.

steps.title: Check the technical base
steps.text: Check indexing (a site: search, and Search Console if you get access), the sitemap and robots.txt, page speed and mobile display, titles and meta descriptions, headings, broken links and duplicate pages. Note each problem with a screenshot.

steps.title: Research keywords
steps.text: List 30 to 50 searches the audience could type, group them by intent (learn, compare, buy) and estimate interest with Google Trends and the search results themselves. Map each group to an existing page or a page to create.

steps.title: Compare with competitors
steps.text: For five key searches, look at the pages that rank first: their format, length, what they answer that the site does not, and who links to them.

steps.title: Write the plan
steps.text: Rank the fixes by impact and effort, and write three content briefs (search intent, title, outline, questions to answer, internal links). Agree with the owner on what to measure in three months.

steps.title: Present it
steps.text: Turn the audit into a short report or slides: the five most important findings first, then the full list.

deliverables: The audit report (PDF or slides) with screenshots
A spreadsheet of keywords grouped by intent and mapped to pages
A one-page summary for the site owner
checklist: Every problem has evidence (a screenshot or a measure)
Fixes are ranked by impact and effort
Keywords are grouped by intent, not just listed
Each brief says which search it answers and how it beats the current results
Recommendations are possible for this owner’s budget and skills
The report starts with the five most important findings
You noted what to measure and when
You asked the owner before publishing anything about their site

cv.bullet: Audited the SEO of [site type] (personal project): [N] technical issues and [N] keyword groups found, prioritised plan and 3 content briefs delivered to the owner; [result after 3 months if you have it].
cv.talk: Explain how you chose what to fix first and why, then walk through one content brief: which search it targets and why the current page does not rank.

stretch: Implement the top fixes with the owner and report the change in impressions and clicks after three months.
Add a local SEO section (Google Business Profile, reviews, local pages).
Write one of the three articles yourself and track its ranking.

projects.title: Which customers say yes? Analysing a bank’s marketing campaigns
projects.summary: Analyse real direct marketing campaigns of a bank: who subscribes, through which contact and after how many calls, and recommend where to focus the next campaign.
projects.why: Marketing analyst interviews ask you to turn campaign data into decisions. This project shows the full chain on real data: clean, segment, compare conversion rates, check that differences are not noise and write recommendations a manager can act on.

data.name: Bank Marketing dataset (UCI)
data.note: Real phone campaigns of a Portuguese bank: client profile, contacts and whether they subscribed. Free, CC BY 4.0.

data.name: Intro to SQL (Kaggle Learn)
data.note: Enough SQL to segment the data, if you prefer SQL to spreadsheets.

data.name: Looker Studio Help
data.note: Build the final report from a Google Sheet, free.

steps.title: Get and understand the data
steps.text: Download the dataset, read its description and list each column: client profile, contact type, month, number of calls in this campaign, previous campaign outcome, and whether the client subscribed (the target).

steps.title: Clean and define the KPIs
steps.text: Handle the unknown values, remove call duration from the analysis (it is only known after the call) and define the KPIs: overall conversion rate, conversion by segment, average number of calls per subscription.

steps.title: Segment
steps.text: Compare conversion by age group, job, contact channel, month, number of calls and previous outcome, in a spreadsheet pivot table or in SQL. Note the segments with high volume and high conversion.

steps.title: Check the differences
steps.text: For the two or three most important differences, check they are not chance: the number of clients behind each rate and a confidence interval or a simple test (the HelloKhedma statistics course explains how).

steps.title: Recommend
steps.text: Write three recommendations with their expected effect, for example the call limit after which conversion collapses, the months to avoid and the segments to target first.

steps.title: Report
steps.text: Build a one-page Looker Studio or spreadsheet report: the KPIs, the funnel, the segment charts and the recommendations.

deliverables: The cleaned dataset and your SQL or spreadsheet with the pivot tables
A short memo with three recommendations and their expected effect
A README explaining the data, the KPIs and the method
checklist: Every KPI has a written definition
Call duration is left out, and you explain why
Rates are shown with the number of clients behind them
At least one difference is checked against chance
Charts have titles that state the finding, not just the variable
Recommendations are specific and say how to measure them
The report fits on one page
The README credits the dataset and its licence

cv.bullet: Analysed [N] contacts of a bank’s direct marketing campaigns (UCI dataset, personal project): conversion by segment, call fatigue point at [N] calls, 3 recommendations to raise conversion by an estimated [X] %.
cv.talk: Explain why call duration must be left out of the analysis, then present your strongest recommendation with the number of clients behind it.

stretch: Build a simple scoring model (logistic regression) and compare it with your segment rules.
Estimate the cost per subscription with a cost per call you assume, and show the most profitable segments.
Present the findings in a 5-minute recorded video.

projects.title: E-commerce funnel and channel dashboard on real GA4 data
projects.summary: Query real Google Analytics 4 data of an online shop in BigQuery, build the purchase funnel by channel and device in Looker Studio, and propose one A/B test with its sample size.
projects.why: Many marketing analytics roles ask for GA4, SQL and dashboards together. Working on the raw event export proves you understand how GA4 data is built, not only how to read its reports, and the A/B test plan shows you can turn findings into an experiment.

data.name: GA4 e-commerce sample dataset
data.note: Three months of real, obfuscated GA4 events from the Google Merchandise Store, in BigQuery.

data.name: BigQuery sandbox
data.note: Query the dataset for free, without a credit card.

data.name: A/B test sample size calculator
data.note: Size the test you propose at the end.

steps.title: Open the dataset
steps.text: Create a free BigQuery sandbox project, open the GA4 sample dataset and read its schema: one row per event, with event_name, event_params, traffic_source, device and ecommerce fields.

steps.title: Build the funnel
steps.text: With SQL, count users at each step (session_start, view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase) over the whole period, then by traffic medium and by device category.

steps.title: Compute the KPIs
steps.text: Conversion rate per step and overall, revenue, average order value and revenue per user, by channel and device. Save the results as small tables.

steps.title: Build the dashboard
steps.text: Connect the result tables to Looker Studio: the funnel, a channel table with conversion and revenue, a device comparison and a date control. Give every chart a title that states the finding.

steps.title: Find the leak and plan a test
steps.text: Pick the step that loses the most users for an important segment, write a hypothesis to fix it, and size an A/B test with the calculator (baseline rate, minimum lift, visitors needed and duration).

steps.title: Document
steps.text: Write a README with the SQL, the KPI definitions, screenshots and the test plan.

deliverables: A one-page test plan with hypothesis, metric, sample size and duration
checklist: Users and events are not confused in the counts
The funnel steps are in the right order and use the same users
Every KPI has a definition
Channel and device breakdowns add up to the total
Charts state the finding in their title
The test has one change, one main metric and a sample size
The README says the data is a public, obfuscated sample
Queries stay inside the free sandbox limits

cv.bullet: Built a GA4 e-commerce funnel and channel dashboard in BigQuery and Looker Studio on [N] M real events (Google Merchandise Store sample, personal project); found the main drop-off at [step] for [segment] and designed an A/B test sized at [N] users.
cv.talk: Explain how the GA4 export stores events and parameters, how you built the funnel in SQL, and why you chose that step for your A/B test.

stretch: Add a cohort analysis of returning buyers.
Compare first-click and last-click attribution by channel.
Automate the result tables with scheduled queries.
